bib.title: Improving language models by retrieving from trillions of tokens

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Improving language models by retrieving from trillions of tokens" (RETRO). Borgeaud, Mensch, Hoffmann, et al. (DeepMind). arXiv:2112.04426v3, 7 Feb 2022. The extraction shows it as a preprint, with no venue printed. Local file: /Users/ramsey-wise/workspace/learn-ai-engineering/generative-ai/02-rag-retrieval/sources/borgeaud-2021-improving-language-models-retrieving-trillions.pdf

COVERAGE: I read all 144,897 chars across 43 pages. That covers the body, references, Appendices A–D, all of F (Tables 14 and 15, Figs 10–12), E.1–E.3, and Table 21's caption. Two parts got less attention. The references I skimmed for where the method comes from. The qualitative sample tables (Tables 16–21, about chars 110k–145k) are colour-coded token grids that come out of the extraction as jumbled columns, so I read only their captions. They contain no numeric results.

CLAIMS
- claim: The headline. With a 2-trillion-token database, the 7.5B RETRO matches GPT-3 and Jurassic-1 on the Pile while using 25× fewer parameters.
  number: 25× (the "×" is dropped in the extraction)
  setup: Comparison against Jurassic-1 (178B), Gopher (280B) and GPT-3 (175B) on the Pile test subsets, in bits-per-byte. The 7.5B RETRO beats Jurassic-1 and Gopher on "a majority" of subsets, not all of them. The authors drop Enron Emails and YouTube Subtitles. The other models' numbers are copied from their own papers (Table 15). The figure also leaves GPT-3 out ("We do not compare against GPT-3 as it is outperformed by Jurassic-1 and Gopher on almost all subsets"), and GPT-3 appears only in Table 15.
  quote: "With a 2 trillion token database, our Retrieval-Enhanced Transformer (RETRO) obtains comparable performance to GPT-3 and Jurassic-1 on the Pile, despite using 25 fewer parameters." / "Overall, RETRO 7.5B outperforms Jurassic-1 and Gopher on a majority of the test sets."
  where: abstract p1; p11–12, Fig 4; Table 15 p35
- claim: Retrieval gives a gain that stays constant across model scale, and the gain is about what you would get from a 10× bigger model without retrieval. The conclusion limits this to "certain datasets".
  number: 10×; 150M–7B parameters
  setup: C4 validation set, bits-per-byte. Model sizes 172M, 425M, 1.5B and 7.5B. Baseline C4 bpb is 0.98/0.92/0.84/0.78 and RETRO[ON] is 0.82/0.77/0.71/0.66 (Table 14).
  quote: "The performance gain of our retrieval models remains constant with model scale (left), and is comparable to multiplying the parameteric model size by 10." / "correspond to non-retrieval models with 10 more parameters on certain datasets"
  where: Fig 1 caption p2; Conclusion p16; Table 14 p34
- claim: Test-set leakage. RETRO exploits overlap between evaluation and training data more than the baselines do. It still beats them on chunks with almost no overlap, and the authors say leakage accounts for only "a modest fraction" of the gain.
  number: α = 12.5% (fewer than 8 contiguous shared tokens)
  setup: The filtered bits-per-byte metric (§2.6). Each 64-token evaluation chunk is matched against its 10 nearest training neighbours using the longest common substring. Tested on C4, Wikitext103, Curation Corpus, Wikipedia Sept 2021 and the Pile (Fig 6; Figs 11 and 12).
  quote: "RETRO models exploit leakage more strongly than baseline models, as indicated by the more negative slope." / "RETRO outperforms baseline models at all leakage levels, down to α = 12.5%. At this level, the loss is computed on chunks with less than 8 contiguous tokens shared with the closest matching chunk" / "only a modest fraction of the gains obtained by RETRO are due to test set leakage"
  where: §4.4 pp14–15; Conclusion p16
- claim: The authors say themselves that the dramatic Wikitext103 numbers are partly leakage.
  number: test perplexity 3.92 (with MassiveText retrieval) against 18.97 (with Wikipedia retrieval) and 22.96 (baseline)
  setup: A RETROfit model fine-tuned from a 24-layer Wikitext103 baseline, with 10 neighbours at evaluation (Table 4).
  quote: "The perplexities for retrieving from full MassiveText are quite low, which is partly due to partial overlap with Wikitext103 not caught by our deduplication." / "RETRO MassiveText (100%) 1792B 28B 3.21 3.92"
  where: Table 4 p12; §4.1 p13
- claim: Retrieval and the training database. They retrieve from 600B tokens during training and from 1.75T tokens at evaluation. To limit leakage, training documents are removed when their 13-gram Jaccard similarity to an evaluation document is 0.8 or higher.
  number: 600B / 1.75T / 0.8
  setup: Multilingual MassiveText, more than 5T tokens in total. Books are subsampled to 4% for the evaluation database.
  quote: "During training (unless otherwise specified), we retrieve from 600B tokens from the training data." / "The evaluation retrieval database thus contains 1.75T tokens." / "remove all training documents with high similarity (0.8 or higher) to a validation or test set document."
  where: §2.1 p3
- claim: How the method works. A frozen BERT retriever finds k-NN chunks (L2 distance, SCaNN). The input is split into 64-token chunks, and each retrieved neighbour is 128 tokens (the chunk plus its continuation). Because the embeddings are frozen, neighbours are precomputed for training. A query takes about 10ms.
  number: n=2048, m=64, r=128; ~10ms
  setup: The 2-trillion-token database.
  quote: "We use n = 2048 and m = 64." / "we can query our 2 trillion token database in 10ms whilst evaluating or sampling from the model"
  where: §2.2–2.3 pp3–4
- claim: Making the database bigger at evaluation keeps improving results. Going from Wikipedia (4B tokens) to all of MassiveText (1.7T) gives "dramatic gains". Models were trained with 2 neighbours. At evaluation the 7B model keeps improving up to 40 neighbours and the 172M model up to 10.
  number: 4B→1.7T; 40 neighbours
  setup: C4 evaluation bpb (Fig 1 middle/right, Table 14). For example, the 7.5B model goes from 0.78 bpb with 2B tokens to 0.66 with the full database.
  quote: "We observe dramatic gains as the retrieval data is increased from Wikipedia (4 billion tokens) to all of Massive text (1.7T tokens)." / "the 172M model improves with up to 10 neighbours, whereas the 7B model improves with up to 40 neighbours."
  where: §4.1 p11; Table 14 p34
- claim: "RETROfitting". You can freeze a pretrained model and train only the new retrieval weights, and get close to a RETRO trained from scratch for about 3% of the pretraining sequences. The model's performance with retrieval switched off stays exactly the same.
  number: <10% of weights; 6M sequences (3%)
  setup: Baselines from 172M to 7B, on MassiveText.
  quote: "training only chunked cross-attention and neighbour encoder parameters (less than 10% of weights for the 7B model) ... requiring only 6 million sequences (3% of the pre-training sequences that we used)."
  where: §4.2 p13
- claim: On question answering, RETRO is competitive with REALM, RAG and DPR but scores below FiD. More than 20 neighbours does not help.
  number: 45.5 EM, against 30.4 closed-book, RAG 44.5, FiD 51.4
  setup: Natural Questions, using the top-20 DPR passages. The 7.5B model is fully fine-tuned for 25k steps.
  quote: "Baseline 7B (closed book) 30.4" / "RETRO 7.5B (DPR retrieval) 45.5" / "underperforms the more recent FiD"
  where: Table 5 p14; §4.3 p14
- claim: The size of the retrieval index. kNN-LM stores one vector per token, so it does not scale to trillions of tokens. RETRO's chunk-level keys do.
  number: 15 TB vs 215 GB (Wikipedia); 93 TB (MassiveText)
  setup: kNN-LM keeps 1024 floats per token.
  quote: "totalling 15 terabytes (Tb) for the 4 billion tokens in Wikipedia ... RETRO only requires 215Gb to index our Wikipedia dataset, and 93Tb for MassiveText."
  where: p13
- claim: The parameters retrieval adds. Each RETRO model is larger than its baseline by +30% at 132M, falling to +8% at 7B.
  number: 6,982M → 7,532M (+8%)
  quote: "6,982M 7,532M (+8%)"
  where: Table 2 p7
- claim: The model's own weights still do work. With retrieval switched off at evaluation (RETRO[OFF]), performance is close to the baseline.
  number: C4 bpb is identical (0.98/0.92/0.84/0.78)
  quote: "At evaluation RETRO can be used without retrieval data (RETRO[OFF]), bringing limited performance degradation compared to baseline transformers."
  where: Fig 1 caption p2; Table 14 p34
- claim: Ablation. Attending to the neighbour alone gives 22% of the retrieval gain, and attending to its continuation gives 56%.
  number: 22% / 56%
  setup: A 247M model trained on 157B tokens, C4 bpb (RETRO 0.822, no retrieval 0.987).
  quote: "attending to neighbours only provides 22% of the performance improvement due to retrieval in RETRO, while attending the future of the neighbours gives 56% of the performance."
  where: App D pp30–31
- claim: Benefits for keeping knowledge current and for privacy. These are argued in the text, not measured. Updating the database is "orders of magnitude cheaper" than retraining, and data can be deleted from the database at inference time.
  number: none
  quote: "To keep retrieval models up-to-date, it may be sufficient to update the retrieval database, which is orders of magnitude cheaper than re-training a model from scratch."
  where: §3.2 p10

LIMITS:
- They do not measure that updating the database keeps the model current or removes data. Those benefits are argued in §3.2 only. The "future" Wikipedia Sept 2021 set (23 articles) shows consistent but small gains: 7.5B bpb goes from 0.65 to 0.61.
- The 25× figure is a comparison of language-model bits-per-byte on the Pile. It is not about downstream tasks, and it holds on "a majority" of subsets only. On dm_mathematics and ubuntu_irc, RETRO does not beat its own 7B baseline. The 10× figure holds "on certain datasets". Curation Corpus shows only a small gain.
- Leakage. Deduplication missed some Wikitext103 overlap, and RETRO "can dramatically exploit such leakage" (Table 19).
- On QA, RETRO trails FiD and does not use the retrieval encoder enough.
- Training RETRO from scratch on the small Wikitext103 dataset overfits.
- §3.2 says retrieval can add bias through which documents get selected.
- The "RETRO" in this paper is retrieval built into pretraining through chunked cross-attention. It is not the RAG pattern of putting retrieved text into the prompt, and Table 3 sets RETRO apart from REALM's "prepend to prompt".
- The paper is from 2021–22. Its comparison models are GPT-3, Jurassic-1 and Gopher, all now superseded.

BUILDS ON: kNN-LM (Khandelwal et al., 2020); continuous cache (Grave et al., 2017); SPALM (Yogatama et al., 2021); DPR (Karpukhin et al., 2020); REALM (Guu et al., 2020); RAG (Lewis et al., 2020); FiD (Izacard and Grave, 2021); EMDR2 (Sachan et al., 2021); BERT (Devlin et al., 2019); ScaNN (Guo et al., 2020); Transformer (Vaswani et al., 2017); MassiveText/Gopher (Rae et al., 2021); leakage concerns from Lee et al. (2021) and Lewis et al. (2021); scaling (Kaplan et al., 2020); retrieval reduces hallucination (Shuster et al., 2021).

CODE: Listing 1 on p27 is a simplified JAX implementation of chunked cross-attention (`multi_chunk_cross_attention`, using `jnp.vectorize`). It is too architecture-specific for this note. The QA prompt format may be useful: "question: {question} \n answer: {answer}", with each neighbour formatted as "title: {title}, source: {source}" (§4.3 p13, §C.4 p29).

FIGURES:
- Fig 1, p2: "Scaling of RETRO. The performance gain of our retrieval models remains constant with model scale (left), and is comparable to multiplying the parameteric model size by 10. The gain increases with the size of the retrieval database (middle) and the number of retrieved neighbours (right)..." This is my candidate. One three-panel image shows the parametric versus non-parametric trade-off: model size, database size and number of neighbours, each against C4 bpb.
- Alternatives: Fig 6, p15 (bpb against the leakage threshold α), which suits a leakage callout. Fig 2, p3, which shows the architecture but is more detail than this note needs.

PROBLEMS:
- In the extraction, small-caps names come out as "R/e.sc /t.sc /r.sc/o.sc" (RETRO), "B/e.sc /r.sc/t.sc" (BERT) and so on. I normalised these in the quotes above, and the rest of each quote is verbatim.
- The extraction drops the "×" glyph. The abstract reads "25 fewer parameters" and the conclusion reads "10 more parameters", so the 25× and 10× multipliers come from context. Check them against the PDF before quoting.
- Decimal points are dropped in some places, for example "𝜆 = 0118" for 0.118 and "1846" for 18.46.
- `figures.py captions` printed nothing, so I took the figure captions from the text extraction.
- Tables 16–21 are garbled.
- The PDF contains no embedded instructions.
